cards.title: Match each campaign promise to the product landing page hero
cards.summary: Repeat the paid ad’s specific promise in the campaign page or PDP hero so shoppers immediately recognize they reached the right offer.
cards.use_when: Launching or diagnosing a paid Meta or Google campaign that sends traffic to a physical-product PDP, collection landing page, or advertorial-to-product journey.
steps: Export the live ad variations and identify the exact promise that earned the click, including qualifying details such as a stated saving, product benefit, use case, or bundle offer.

Make that promise the primary hero headline on the corresponding destination page rather than replacing it with a generic brand line. For example, an ad focused on a three-pack saving should arrive at a page that leads with that three-pack value.
Use the supporting line to explain how the product delivers the benefit: material, format, ingredient, construction, compatibility, or other genuine mechanism. Do not merely restate the headline.
Build separate landing-page hero variants when distinct ad angles target different needs or products; do not force all traffic through one vague message.
Audit the page whenever creative changes, especially after adding a new acquisition angle.
Place the purchase path and core reassurance in the first screen: product context, price or offer clarity, purchase CTA, and applicable shipping, warranty, or return information.
caveats: The source treats above-the-fold visibility as especially important and states that many visitors do not scroll, but its scrolling figures are heuristics rather than universal benchmarks.
Only make claims that the product, evidence, and local advertising rules support.

cards.title: Build a physical-product hero around outcome, mechanism, proof, and reassurance
cards.summary: A product hero should pair a clear customer outcome with an honest explanation of how the item delivers it, a direct purchase action, relevant proof, and friction reducers.
cards.use_when: Designing the above-the-fold portion of a PDP or dedicated single-product campaign page for cold traffic.
steps: Write a benefit-led headline that identifies the shopper outcome or use-case instead of describing the company. Keep claims specific and supportable.

Use a subheadline to explain the mechanism: what the product is, how it works, why its materials or design matter, or what makes the bundle useful. The subheadline should add information rather than echo the headline.
Use an action-oriented purchase control such as “Choose your size,” “Build your bundle,” or “Add [product] to cart,” rather than a vague CTA.
Position genuine friction reducers close to the purchase action: shipping terms, return window, warranty, secure payment, compatibility guidance, or a legitimate guarantee.
Use product imagery or video that demonstrates the claimed use, outcome, scale, or contents—not decorative imagery that fails to clarify the offer.

Add relevant, authentic proof such as verified customer feedback, substantiated editorial coverage, or review ratings. If using publication logos, pair them with a real attributable statement when permission and context allow.
If multiple proof types appear, ensure each resolves a different concern rather than duplicating decorative badges.
caveats: The source’s preference for stacking two forms of social proof reflects its agency experience, not a guaranteed lift.
Do not imply endorsements, fabricate reviews, or present generic logos as evidence of product performance.

cards.title: Remove navigation leaks from single-offer campaign pages
cards.summary: For paid traffic sent to one product or bundle offer, minimize header exits so the shopper’s next decision is to evaluate and buy that offer.
cards.use_when: Creating a dedicated paid-traffic landing page for a hero product, seasonal kit, limited collection, replenishment offer, or bundle.
steps: Define the one primary conversion event for the page, usually add to cart, bundle selection, or checkout initiation.
Remove the full storefront navigation from the dedicated campaign template so visitors cannot immediately divert to broad category, editorial, account, or blog pages.
Retain only controls needed to complete a confident purchase, such as a visible logo, cart access, customer support link where necessary, and the primary purchase CTA.
Make key product details, variant selection, price, offer terms, and reassurance accessible on the page so reduced navigation does not trap a shopper who needs decision information.
Check mobile carefully: ensure the minimized header does not crowd the CTA, obscure price, or push product context below the first screen.
Keep normal navigation on the broader storefront, category pages, and homepage when product discovery and comparison are the intended shopping behavior.
caveats: This is for dedicated, single-offer campaign pages, not a blanket recommendation to strip navigation from an ecommerce storefront.
If a product requires extensive comparison, compatibility research, or service documentation, provide those decision aids within the campaign path.

cards.title: Use problem–agitate–solve to connect a product to a real shopper need
cards.summary: On cold-traffic product pages, name the shopper’s existing problem, briefly establish its consequence, and immediately show the product’s credible solution.
cards.use_when: Writing the first explanatory section below the hero of a PDP, advertorial-to-product page, or product-focused campaign landing page.
steps: Place the section directly after the initial offer and product overview, where a new visitor needs a reason the item matters.
Describe a recognizable customer problem in the customer’s language: an inconvenient routine, poor fit, storage issue, unreliable product experience, or other genuine pain point.
Agitate only enough to make the consequence concrete—lost time, wasted product, discomfort, repeat replacement, or frustrating setup—without resorting to fear tactics or unsupported harm claims.
Pivot immediately to the product’s specific solution and mechanism. Explain which feature, design choice, material, contents, or usage method addresses the problem.
Use visual demonstrations, concise benefit bullets, and authentic use cases to make the connection easy to scan.
Review every factual, comparative, and performance statement for substantiation before publishing; AI-generated draft language must not introduce invented statistics or claims.
caveats: The source positions PAS as useful for cold traffic; it may be unnecessary when shoppers already arrive with high product knowledge or strong purchase intent.
Avoid medical, diagnostic, or exaggerated root-cause claims unless they are properly supported and compliant.

cards.title: Make product-page headings and CTA lead-ins understandable to skimmers
cards.summary: Assume many visitors scan rather than read, so each heading, image, and repeated CTA must communicate the product value without relying on dense body copy.
cards.use_when: Editing a long PDP or campaign page with vague section labels, low CTA engagement, or text-heavy feature explanations.
steps: Read every section heading without its body copy. Rewrite headings that do not communicate a customer benefit, proof point, product use, or reason to continue.
Replace internal labels and empty prompts such as “The details” or “Ready for your next step?” with useful statements such as “Keeps your carry-on organized without bulky compartments,” where true.
Break long paragraphs into short blocks and place the most important benefit or qualification first. The source flags long multi-line paragraphs as likely to bury important content.
Repeat the same primary purchase CTA after major decision sections—such as product benefits, demonstration, reviews, bundle choice, and guarantee—so a convinced shopper need not scroll back to buy.
Keep CTA labels tied to the purchase task: choose a variant, select a bundle, add to cart, or buy now.
Use the product images and headings to carry the core argument for scanners, while retaining accurate supporting detail for readers.
caveats: The source’s read-versus-scan split and claim that more buttons improve conversion are heuristics, not universal measurements.
Repeated CTAs should not bypass required choices such as size, shade, subscription frequency, or compatibility confirmation.

cards.title: Close a long product landing page with a purchase recap
cards.summary: Treat the bottom of a product campaign page as a final decision block that restates the value, offer, and purchase reassurance before the shopper leaves.
cards.use_when: Building a long-form single-product, bundle, launch, or seasonal campaign page that ends weakly after reviews, FAQs, or product education.
steps: Create a visually distinct closing block rather than ending abruptly in footer navigation.
Restate the central customer outcome and summarize the two or three strongest reasons to choose the product or bundle.
Repeat the exact offer in clear commercial terms: selected product, quantity or bundle, price context where appropriate, and any genuine promotion conditions.
Add the same purchase control used above, allowing the shopper to select required variants or return to the configured add-to-cart module.
Place meaningful reassurance near the CTA: shipping timing, returns, warranty, payment options, or a truthful satisfaction guarantee.
Use a product image, concise demonstration asset, or customer proof that reinforces the final decision; do not add unrelated content merely to fill the page.
Check that any urgency is real and that promotion end dates, inventory statements, and savings claims are accurate.
caveats: The source presents this closing structure as a framework rather than an A/B-validated universal layout.
A short PDP may not need a separate closer if the sticky purchase module and core purchase information remain accessible.

cards.title: Optimize the ecommerce homepage for product discovery using View Product Rate
cards.summary: Treat the homepage as a route into merchandise and monitor how effectively it moves visitors from brand context into actual product views.
cards.use_when: Auditing a store homepage when traffic is arriving but category and PDP sessions, add-to-carts, or revenue are weak.
steps: Measure View Product Rate: the share of homepage visitors who proceed to a product page. Use it alongside downstream add-to-cart and purchase metrics so higher product views do not conceal worse-quality traffic.
Make the homepage headline state the shopper-facing benefit or merchandising promise rather than leaving the value proposition buried in supporting copy.

Choose lead imagery that supports the intended emotional outcome and product category. For a pet brand positioned around happier pets, use imagery that communicates that promise rather than imagery that suggests the opposite.
Make top discovery choices visual. Test category tiles, icons, or product images beside category labels instead of relying only on text dropdowns.
Limit top-level menu choices enough to keep navigation legible; the source suggests seven or fewer as a practical heuristic, not a fixed rule.
Test visual navigation by device and category. The source reports a 15% conversion lift in one pet-client image-navigation test, which is a case example rather than an expected outcome.
caveats: View Product Rate is a discovery metric, not a substitute for revenue, conversion rate, or contribution-margin analysis.
Menu item count and visual-navigation results vary by catalog breadth and customer shopping intent.

cards.title: Put purchase-critical PDP information in a scannable first screen
cards.summary: Make the product gallery, identity, rating, options, add-to-cart path, and key reassurance easy to find before shoppers must scroll.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a PDP above the fold, especially on mobile, where shoppers struggle to understand the product or reach the add-to-cart control.
steps: Expose the product gallery with visible thumbnails or another clear gallery control rather than relying only on subtle carousel dots; shoppers should be able to see that more product views exist.
Keep product identity and credible review information prominent near the gallery. Test the precise ordering for your category, but do not bury either below long descriptive copy.
Surface the information needed to make a purchase decision: price, variant or quantity selection, availability where relevant, and the Add to Cart control.
Keep purchase reassurance close to the button, such as legitimate free-shipping thresholds, return policy, warranty, secure checkout, or delivery expectations.
Translate dense feature copy into short benefit-led bullets, supported by icons or imagery, while preserving links to full specifications and care instructions for detail-oriented buyers.
Review both desktop and mobile layouts. On mobile, verify that gallery controls, option selectors, price, and the cart action are not separated by excessive scrolling.
caveats: The source has strong hierarchy preferences derived from its framework; exact ordering of title, rating, and purchase controls should be validated with your own users and analytics.
Do not hide legally required pricing, subscription conditions, or material/product disclosures in the name of a cleaner first screen.

cards.title: State bundle savings so shoppers never need to calculate them
cards.summary: Put the exact monetary saving in each bundle option so customers can immediately compare quantity choices and see the reason to trade up.
cards.use_when: Merchandising multipacks, buy-more-save-more offers, starter kits, replenishment quantities, or volume discounts on a PDP or campaign page.
steps: Calculate each option’s total price, per-unit price where helpful, and exact saving versus purchasing the same units individually.
Name the saving directly in the bundle label, such as “3-pack — save $20,” rather than showing only a reduced total that requires mental arithmetic.
Display options side by side or in a clear vertical comparison that makes the increasing value obvious. Include quantity, total price, savings, and any recurring-purchase terms.
Make the saving legible on mobile; do not rely on faint, small, or below-the-fold discount text.
Ensure the shopper can tell which option is selected and that the cart accurately reflects the selected quantity and saving.

A/B test explicit-savings labels against your existing presentation, monitoring not only conversion but also bundle mix, average order value, margin, returns, and subscription cancellation if applicable.
caveats: The source says it has tested this approach but supplies no lift figure; treat it as an experiment rather than a guaranteed conversion tactic.
Savings must be calculated against a legitimate reference price and shown in accordance with applicable pricing and promotional rules.

cards.title: Convert dense product information into visual benefit modules
cards.summary: Turn long specification blocks into image-led, icon-supported benefit modules that help scanners understand why a feature matters.
cards.use_when: Reworking a PDP, collection landing page, or product campaign page dominated by paragraphs about materials, specifications, ingredients, construction, or features.
steps: Locate text-heavy blocks that require a shopper to read several sentences before learning the product benefit.
For each feature, write the customer-facing consequence first. For example, present a construction detail as the durability, cleaning, packing, comfort, or performance benefit it credibly enables.
Build a compact module with a relevant product visual, an icon or visual cue where useful, a concise benefit headline, and one short supporting explanation.
Use imagery that demonstrates the feature in use, material detail, scale, or before-and-after setup where authentic; avoid decorative visuals that add no product understanding.
Repeat this format across key value propositions so the page develops a consistent scan path.
Retain accessible full specifications, dimensions, ingredients, compatibility, safety details, and care information for shoppers who need them before purchase.
caveats: The source’s preference for scannable visual presentation is based on a scanning heuristic, not proof that all audiences avoid detailed copy.
Do not convert factual requirements into vague benefits; regulated disclosures and material details must remain complete and accurate.

cards.title: Audit proof and best-practice elements for decision impact
cards.summary: Testimonials, badges, guarantees, and media logos help only when they answer a real shopper question and reinforce the product’s actual value proposition.
cards.use_when: A PDP or campaign page has reviews, trust badges, and press logos but still feels generic or produces weak add-to-cart and purchase performance.
steps: Inventory every proof and reassurance element on the page: reviews, ratings, user photos, press logos, claims, badges, shipping messages, guarantees, and FAQs.
For each element, state the customer doubt it is meant to resolve: performance, fit, quality, delivery risk, return risk, legitimacy, or value. Rework or remove elements with no clear job.
Select authentic customer reviews that describe the same outcome or use case promised by the headline, rather than using generic praise that could apply to anything.
If using press or retailer logos, include an authorized, attributable quote or specific context when available instead of a bare “as seen in” strip.
Replace filler headings and decorative trust components with product-specific proof, demonstration, or clear policy language.
Prioritize improvements that make existing elements more meaningful before adding another generic badge or logo row.
caveats: This is the presenter’s audit principle, not an empirical rule that every proof element must visibly change conversion.
Never alter reviews to manufacture outcomes, imply unsupported endorsements, or use guarantees that the business will not honor.

input.source_name: I Studied 1,000 Landing Pages, This Stops Them Making Money.docx

cards.title: Match the ad's exact promise to the landing page headline
cards.summary: Whatever specific, quantifiable claim won the click must be the first thing the visitor reads above the fold, or they bounce.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a paid-traffic landing page (Google or Meta) before or during a campaign to fix high bounce and low conversion from ad clicks.
steps: Pull the exact ad copy that generated the traffic — e.g. an ad promising 'Lose 6-20 lbs in 2-4 weeks' — and compare it word-for-word against the page headline.
Replace generic brand headlines ('Retreat to a new reality') with the same benefit and number the ad used, so the visitor instantly confirms they landed in the right place.
Treat the above-the-fold as the only section 100% of visitors see; the source states roughly 60% never scroll past it, so the core offer must live there.
If you run multiple ad angles, build a matching headline variant per angle rather than sending all traffic to one generic page.
Re-check congruence every time you rotate a new ad angle into the account.
caveats: The '60% never scroll' and '100% see above the fold' figures are the source's stated heuristics, not a universal measured benchmark for your store.

cards.title: Structure the above-the-fold anatomy for lead-gen pages
cards.summary: A high-converting hero section stacks a benefit headline, mechanism sub-headline, FUD reducers, a benefit-driven CTA, reinforcing imagery and social proof.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the top screen of a lead-gen, B2B or service landing page where the goal is form fills or booked calls.
steps: Write a headline that states the dream outcome ('lose fat fast'), not the company description.
Write a sub-headline that explains HOW you deliver the headline promise — unique mechanism, proprietary method or program steps — instead of repeating the headline.
Make the CTA button benefit-driven ('Gain muscle fast', 'Get thicker hair now') rather than generic ('Contact us', 'Schedule your free analysis'); the source calls 'contact us' overused and weak.
Place FUD reducers (fear, uncertainty, doubt) right beside the CTA: money-back guarantee, free trial, no surgery or pills, free shipping.
Use an image or video that reinforces the value prop (a transformation shot) rather than a generic facility photo.

Stack two forms of social proof — e.g. a real review plus a named-media quote — because the source says A/B testing showed two outperform one; a bare 'as seen on' logo row is overdone, so add an actual quote beneath the logo.
caveats: The two-social-proof and benefit-CTA claims are the presenter's agency's experience across 400+ pages, not a guaranteed lift for every niche.

cards.title: Remove navigation leaks on dedicated landing pages
cards.summary: Kill the top navigation bar on campaign pages so traffic cannot wander off to About, Explore or Blog before converting.
cards.use_when: Setting up any dedicated ad landing page (lead-gen, course, or single-offer ecommerce campaign page) where one conversion action is the goal.
steps: Decide the single conversion event for the page (form submit, call booking, add to cart) and make it the only exit you want.
Delete or visually suppress the site-wide navigation bar so visitors can't leave via About, Explore, Blog or category links.
Keep only the logo (linking home is optional) and the primary CTA in the header zone.
Verify on mobile, where the source focuses its audits, that the menu isn't hiding the CTA or pushing the offer below the fold.
Reserve full navigation for the main site and homepages where browsing is the goal — don't strip it everywhere.
caveats: This applies to dedicated paid-traffic landing pages; the source doesn't recommend removing navigation from a browsable storefront where category discovery drives revenue.

cards.title: Use the PAS framework in the post-hero pain section
cards.summary: For cold ad traffic, open the mid-page with Problem-Agitate-Solve so the copy names the struggle and immediately ties it to the unique solution.
cards.use_when: Writing the section right below the hero on a cold-traffic landing page (Meta/Google) where visitors don't know your brand yet.
steps: Place a pain-point section directly after the hero — the source's page framework puts pain right below the value prop.
Name the problem the visitor already feels (e.g. thinning hair in the mirror, shedding).
Agitate it briefly to raise emotional stakes without turning to fear-mongering.
Immediately pivot to the solve: your unique mechanism and how it resolves the specific pain.
Avoid pages that only list pain points with no solution attached — the source calls the pain-only version a common miss.
Use AI copy prompts only as a first draft, then edit for your actual mechanism and claims.
caveats: The source says its own AI-generated examples were placeholders; replace fabricated stats and claims with real, compliant ones before publishing.

cards.title: Make headlines readable on their own
cards.summary: Assume visitors read only headlines, so every section headline must communicate the benefit without the body copy.
cards.use_when: Editing landing page section headlines and CTA lead-ins, or diagnosing pages with vague headers like 'Analysis first' or 'Ready for your first step?'
steps: Read each headline in isolation and ask whether it names a concrete benefit or reason to act; rewrite anything a skimmer can't decode.
Write section headlines as benefit statements, not internal labels or rhetorical questions ('Ready for your first step?' gives no why).
Repeat the primary CTA button throughout every critical section rather than once at the bottom — the source claims more buttons increase conversion likelihood.
Compress over-long body copy (the source flags 8-line paragraphs as pushing key content below the fold) to 2-3 sentences max per block.
Sanity-check with the source's 80/20 rule: assume ~20% read copy and 80% scan, so headlines and visuals must carry the message.
caveats: The 20/80 read-vs-scan split and 'more buttons = more conversion' are the presenter's stated heuristics, not universal measured facts.

cards.title: Add a closing recap section at the page bottom
cards.summary: Treat the footer area as a mini above-the-fold that recaps value, restates the offer and reduces doubt one final time.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing the bottom of a lead-gen or course landing page where drop-off happens before the last CTA.
steps: Create a 'closer' block modeled on the hero: final value recap, three value props, CTA button, FUD reducers and an image, video or form.
Give one final reason to act today instead of a weak line like 'Want to know more?'.
Repeat the benefit-driven CTA that matches the hero button so the page ends on the same action.
Include the form or booking element inside the closer to capture visitors who scrolled the whole way.
Keep it visually distinct as a contained block so it reads as a deliberate summary, not stray footer links.
caveats: The source describes this as its own framework, not an A/B-validated result.

cards.title: Offer one core action per lead-gen page
cards.summary: Competing offers split attention; pick a single conversion action and reduce up-front friction.
cards.use_when: Auditing a lead-gen page that shows two CTAs (e.g. 'schedule a free analysis' and 'get your free guide') or requires booking a call immediately.
steps: Count the distinct offers and CTAs on the page; if there's more than one core action, cut down to the single best-converting action.
For cold Meta/Google traffic, lower up-front friction by collecting simple info via a form instead of demanding a full call booking.
Move a call-booking calendar to a later step after the lead is captured, if you still want a call.
Ensure the remaining CTA is benefit-driven, not a generic service label.
Re-audit after edits to confirm no secondary offer (guide, newsletter, second form) has crept back in.
caveats: The presenter's preference for forms over instant call booking is a positioning choice for cold traffic, not a rule that works for every funnel or high-intent offer.

cards.title: Convert transactional course pages into outcome-driven offers
cards.summary: Sell the transformation and career outcome, not the format and duration, then stack value so the price feels like a no-brainer.
cards.use_when: Writing the above-the-fold and offer sections of a digital product, course or certificate sales page.
steps: Replace format-style titles ('Dual health and life coach certificate', 'Digital imaging technician course') with the end outcome buyers care about ('Land six-figure DIT gigs, travel the world, work on global sets').
Move transactional specs (online, self-paced, 5 months, 3-5 hours/week) out of the hero and into supporting detail.
Enumerate exactly what's included — modules, video counts, completion certificates, module-by-module contents — so the offer is fully legible.
Apply value stacking: assign a dollar value to each bonus and module, show the total, and present the bundled price against that stack.
Position the whole package as one price for a large list of inclusions, whether the ticket is high or low.
Keep the presentation concrete rather than a vague 'who is this for' laundry list.
caveats: The 'felt like a no-brainer' outcome is the source's framing from its own client work, not a measured conversion result.

cards.title: Diagnose ecommerce homepage by View Product Rate
cards.summary: The homepage's job is to move visitors to product pages, so optimize for the share who view a product.
cards.use_when: Reviewing store homepage performance when category and product page traffic is under target.
steps: Measure View Product Rate — the presenter calls it the most under-indexed metric on the store homepages it audits.
Rewrite the homepage headline to state the customer benefit instead of burying it in sub-copy no one reads.
Choose imagery that reinforces the emotional promise (smiling pets for happy-pet positioning, not under-the-weather shots).
Replace text-only dropdowns with icons or images beside category items; the source reports a 15% conversion lift from an image-navigation A/B test for a pet client.
Keep the number of top-level menu items at or under seven to avoid analysis paralysis and site exits.
Retest menu imagery per niche before rolling out store-wide.
caveats: The 15% lift and 'seven items' threshold are source-specific A/B and agency observations, not universal benchmarks — validate on your own traffic.

cards.title: Fix PDP image and information hierarchy above the fold
cards.summary: Expose thumbnails, lead with the title, surface reviews and keep add-to-cart with FUD reducers in the first screen.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an ecommerce product page and its above-the-fold layout.
steps: Replace hidden carousel dots with visible image thumbnails so shoppers see the full gallery immediately.
Order the hierarchy title-first, then reviews — not reviews below the title — because on landing pages reviews are placed first.
Fit as much purchase-critical info above the fold as possible; the source draws a 'red line' and says everything above it should be visible without scrolling.
Keep the Add to Cart button and its FUD reducers together: money-back guarantee, warranty, free shipping.
Break long body copy into icon-supported benefit bullets, since the source assumes most visitors scan rather than read.
Confirm the layout on mobile as well as desktop.
caveats: Hierarchy preferences (reviews above title) come from the source's framework and testing, not a universal rule for every category.

cards.title: Don't make shoppers do bundle math
cards.summary: State the exact dollar saving in the bundle headline instead of showing only a discounted price.
cards.use_when: Designing bundle offers and quantity-break pricing on an ecommerce product page.
steps: Identify bundle options (2-pack, 3-pack) and calculate the exact amount saved per bundle.
Put the saving in the bundle title itself — '3-Pack: Save $20', 'One pack save €10, Two pack save €22' — rather than hiding it in small price text.
Make the saving visually prominent on mobile; the source flags discounts that are invisible on a phone as a key miss.
Compare bundles side by side so the shopper sees the escalating saving without arithmetic.
A/B test headline saving amounts against standard discounted-price displays.
caveats: The source reports testing this but does not publish a specific lift figure; treat as a hypothesis to validate on your own store.

cards.title: Turn dense product copy into scannable visuals
cards.summary: Break long product-information blocks into icon-driven, image-led value props that skimmers actually consume.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a product page or landing page section that currently uses large paragraphs of specification text.
steps: Identify the biggest blocks of undifferentiated text on the page — specs, features, materials.
Extract the benefit of each feature and present it as a short icon-plus-line item.
Pair each benefit with imagery so the section is visual rather than prose.
Repeat this treatment across the page's value prop sections rather than one hero-only fix.
Keep some text for the minority who read, but lead with scannable structure.
caveats: The read/scan split behind this is the source's stated heuristic, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Judge best-practice tactics by impact, not checkbox compliance
cards.summary: Implementing a tactic without making it impactful still fails; e.g. a generic testimonial or generic 'as seen on' logos solve nothing.
cards.use_when: Auditing a page that claims to follow best practices (testimonials, logos, guarantees) but still converts poorly.
steps: List each 'best practice' element on the page and ask what specific doubt or desire it resolves.
Replace generic testimonials with ones that mirror the core value prop and outcome.
Replace bare 'as seen on' logo rows with an actual quote from the featured source.
Replace filler headlines like 'Analysis first, then focus' with benefit-driven statements.
If an element adds no impact, remove or rework it rather than keeping it for appearance.
Apply this filter to every section before adding new tactics.
caveats: This is the presenter's critique from auditing client pages, not an empirical study; use judgment per brand.

cards.title: Reuse ad-to-page congruence and hero anatomy for digital product pages
cards.summary: The lead-gen hero framework (benefit headline, mechanism sub-headline, FUD reducers, CTA, social proof) transfers to course and product pages.
cards.use_when: Adapting a proven lead-gen hero structure to a digital product or course sales page during a redesign.
steps: Overlay the same anatomy on the course page: outcome headline, how-we-deliver sub-headline, two social proofs, benefit CTA, doubt reducers.
Add the ad's exact promise to the hero when the course page receives paid traffic.
Update CTA copy from transactional ('Enroll now') to outcome-driven where it fits the brand.
Place guarantee or refund terms close to the purchase button as the FUD reducer.
Roll the same structure down the page into each value section rather than only fixing the hero.
caveats: The source notes overlap between B2B, digital-product and ecommerce pages but presents this as its own framework, not a validated universal layout.
